sub: From the beginning of the universe to the new heavens and new earth: eight units that reveal God's eternal power and divine nature.

units.title: The Universe Had a Beginning
units.sub: The most stunning discovery of twentieth-century astronomy echoes the very first sentence of the Bible.

blocks.h: If you filmed the whole history of the universe and then pressed “rewind,” what would you see?
Every galaxy would run backward, drawing closer and closer together, until they were all squeezed into one hot, dense starting point. Before that moment, our telescopes can see nothing at all.
In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

More than three thousand years ago, Moses wrote the first sentence of the Bible. Twentieth-century astronomers spent decades, using the best instruments available, to reach the same conclusion: the universe has not always existed. The universe had a beginning.
The galaxies are moving apart

Astronomers found that the light from distant galaxies is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum. This is called “redshift.” Redshift means a galaxy is moving away from us, and the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is receding.

Picture a loaf of raisin bread still rising in the oven. As the dough swells, every raisin sees all the other raisins moving away from it, and the farther away a raisin is, the faster it recedes. The universe is like that dough: the galaxies are not flying apart through space; space itself is expanding.

Beginning in 1912, American astronomer Vesto Slipher measured redshifts in the spectra of most spiral nebulae. In 1927, Belgian physicist Georges Lemaître derived from Einstein's equations that the universe is expanding; he was also a Catholic priest. In 1929, Edwin Hubble confirmed with observational data that a galaxy's distance is proportional to its speed of recession. In 2018, the International Astronomical Union recommended renaming this law the “Hubble–Lemaître law.”
The afterglow of the beginning

If the universe began hot and dense, some “leftover warmth” should remain today. In 1965, while calibrating an antenna at Bell Labs, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson unexpectedly picked up a faint microwave hiss coming evenly from every direction. It was that very afterglow, now called the “cosmic microwave background radiation.” The two men received the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

It is like walking into a house after a great fire has gone out: you can no longer see the flames, but the walls are still faintly warm. Today this afterglow has cooled to about minus 270 degrees Celsius, yet it still fills the whole sky evenly.

In the 1990s, the COBE satellite measured the spectrum of this radiation and found it matched the predicted “blackbody” curve almost perfectly, at a temperature of about 2.725 K. Another independent line of evidence is the lightest elements in the universe: by mass, ordinary matter is about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium, exactly the ratio predicted by the “hot beginning” model.
Scientists did not welcome this discovery at first

In 1917, Einstein added a “cosmological constant” to his equations to keep the universe static and unchanging. British astronomer Fred Hoyle proposed the “steady-state theory,” which held that the universe had no beginning, and on a 1949 BBC radio program he mockingly called his rivals' theory the “Big Bang,” a name that has stuck ever since. Only after the background radiation was discovered did the steady-state theory lose the support of most scholars.

Robert Jastrow, founding director of NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies and a self-described agnostic, wrote in his book God and the Astronomers that the scientist has scaled the mountains of ignorance and is about to conquer the highest peak, only to be greeted by a band of theologians who have been sitting there for centuries.
We look at each claim separately and mark how certain it is. Keeping scientific fact and philosophical inference distinct is a way of honoring the truth.
The universe is expanding: distant galaxies are generally redshifted, and the farther away they are, the greater the redshift.
The cosmic microwave background radiation exists, with a temperature of about 2.725 K and a spectrum that is a nearly perfect blackbody.
The history of the observable universe can be traced back to an extremely hot, extremely dense early state.

According to the standard cosmological model, the universe is about 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years old. Different methods still give different values for the expansion rate (the Hubble constant); this is called the “Hubble tension,” and researchers are still studying it.

Time and space themselves have an absolute beginning. In 2003, Borde, Guth and Vilenkin proved that a universe that has, on average, always been expanding cannot be extended infinitely into the past. But what happens at the scale of quantum gravity is still unsettled, and some scholars have proposed other models.

Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause. This is the philosophical “kalam cosmological argument,” and its second premise is supported by the scientific discoveries above.
Perspectives Room

Evangelical Christians hold different views on “how old the universe is,” but they are completely united that “the universe had a beginning and was created by God.” Below is an overview of the two main views; scholars from each position will review the wording in the future.

items.h: Accepts the age of the universe measured by astronomy, and holds that the “days” of Genesis 1 can be understood as long periods of time or as a literary framework.

Based on the genealogies of Genesis and the literal meaning of “day,” holds that the universe is thousands of years old, and offers a different interpretation of the assumptions behind astronomical age measurements.

blocks.h: We are united on the core and gracious on the secondary matters. Brothers and sisters of different views can all marvel together here: the universe did not come from itself.

For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse.
His eternal power: something from nothing

Everything human beings make is a rearrangement of materials that already exist. Only God can bring “something” out of “nothing.” A universe that began to exist points to a cause outside the universe, one of immeasurable power.
By Yahweh's word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth. … For he spoke, and it was done. He commanded, and it stood firm.
By faith, we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible.
His divine nature: before time
The cause of the universe cannot be part of the universe. This One must transcend time, space and matter, and must have chosen to create by his own will. The Bible tells us who he is:
Before the mountains were born, before you had formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God.
They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same. Your years will have no end.

The second law of thermodynamics says that the usable energy in the universe keeps decreasing, like a garment slowly wearing out. Three thousand years ago the psalmist already painted this picture, and set it against a God who “is the same.”
The Lord of creation is Jesus Christ

For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, … all things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.

The Lord who existed before the universe began entered time for our sake, became a man, died on the cross and rose from the dead. The Creator is not only the cause of the universe; he is the Savior who longs to draw near to us.
Please put down your phone for two minutes. If you can see the sky tonight, walk to the window and look up. Use your heart, not just your head.
When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him?
Reflect: The Lord who created hundreds of billions of galaxies also knows my name. Who am I before him?

Prayer: Lord, you are the beginning of all things. I confess that I often want to be my own lord. Today I return to my proper place as a creature: I let you be God, and I let you reign in my heart. All glory belongs to you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
You may follow this with a hymn praising the Creator, such as “How Great Thou Art.”
321 Life Application

items: Change your perspective: from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one. My troubles are big, but the God who created the universe is bigger.
Return to our proper place: pride is leaving our place and trying to take God's. Under the starry sky I learn humility: letting people be people, and letting God be God.
Let Jesus reign: all things are held together in him, so I hand my life over to his rule too.

blocks.h: This week: pick one evening to look up at the sky for five minutes. Then send the share card below to a friend and ask, “Where do you think the universe came from?”
Quiz

quiz.q: What did Hubble's observations show in 1929?
o: The farther a galaxy is, the faster it moves away from us
The universe is static and unchanging
The sun revolves around the earth
quiz.e: Distance is proportional to the speed of recession, which shows that the universe is expanding.

quiz.q: Which analogy best fits the cosmic microwave background radiation?
o: The warmth left in the walls after a great fire goes out
Static given off by the earth's magnetic field
quiz.e: It is the afterglow left by the universe's hot beginning, now cooled to about 2.7 K.

quiz.q: Which statement below is a “philosophical inference” rather than a direct scientific observation?
o: The spectra of distant galaxies are redshifted
The background radiation has a temperature of about 2.7 K
The beginning of the universe requires a cause beyond space and time
quiz.e: The first two are observations; the third is an inference drawn from them. We honestly keep them distinct.

share.v: By faith, we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible.

units.title: A Just-Right Universe
units.sub: If a few numbers in the laws of physics were even slightly different, there would be no stars, no planets and no life.

share.v: He has made the earth by his power. He has established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding has he stretched out the heavens.

blocks.h: Imagine a control panel for the universe with dozens of dials on it: the strength of gravity, the strength of electromagnetism, the mass ratio of the proton to the electron…
Physicists have found that if several of these dials were turned even a tiny bit, the universe would have no stable stars, no carbon, and no us.
By wisdom Yahweh founded the earth. By understanding, he established the heavens.
The cosmological constant: the most astonishing number

The “cosmological constant” (dark energy) that drives the universe's accelerating expansion is extremely small. By rough estimates from quantum physics, it ought to be about 10<sup>120</sup> times larger. Physicist Steven Weinberg pointed out that if it were a few hundred times larger than its actual value, the universe would expand too quickly for galaxies ever to form.

It is like shooting an arrow from earth and hitting a bull's-eye smaller than the eye of a needle on the far side of the universe. The value of the cosmological constant lands right in that bull's-eye.
Other just-right numbers

items: The ratio of gravity to electromagnetism: determines whether stars can burn steadily for a long time.
The strong nuclear force: the force that binds atomic nuclei together; its strength affects whether the chemical elements can form.
Density fluctuations in the early universe: about one part in 100,000. Too small, and matter could not clump into galaxies; too large, and most of it would collapse into black holes.
The dimensions of space: three-dimensional space allows both planetary orbits and atoms to remain stable.

blocks.h: Britain's Astronomer Royal, Martin Rees, picked out six numbers that determine the shape of the universe in his book Just Six Numbers. Astrophysicist Luke Barnes, in a 2012 review paper, surveyed many published studies on fine-tuning.

Scholars still debate the degree of “fine-tuning”: some constants can change together and offset one another, and some estimates depend on particular models. But most physicists agree that, under the present laws of physics, the range that permits life is very narrow compared with the range of possible values.
The universe's expansion is accelerating, and the cosmological constant (or dark energy) driving it is very small but not zero.
If the cosmological constant were several hundred times larger, galaxies would have difficulty forming.
For several physical constants, the range that permits life is quite narrow; the degree of fine-tuning of individual constants and the methods of calculation are still debated by scholars.
Perspectives Room: How do we explain fine-tuning?

items.h: The values of the universe look carefully set, pointing to a wise and purposeful Designer. This is a philosophical inference drawn from observation.

Perhaps there are countless universes, each with different values, and we happen to be in one that fits. For now this remains theoretical speculation with no direct observational evidence, and the mechanism that would produce a multiverse itself needs fine-tuning.

blocks.h: Whichever explanation one takes, both admit that the universe's values “look as if they have been tuned.” The question is: is this coincidence, one universe among countless others, or the intention of a Designer?
He has made the earth by his power. He has established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding has he stretched out the heavens.
His divine nature: boundless wisdom
A precise clock points to a clockmaker; a just-right universe points to a Creator of infinite wisdom. He did not merely make all things; he arranged the universe just right for life, and for us.
Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you establish its dominion over the earth?

Out of the whirlwind, God asked Job a whole series of questions about heaven and earth. When Job understood, he said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” Grasping the precision of the universe can move us from knowing about God to meeting God.
For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.
Think about it: the largest and the smallest numbers in the universe are all tuned just right in his hands. Your life is in his hands too.
Reflect: What is one thing in my life that I thought was chance, but was really God's arrangement?
Prayer: Lord, in your wisdom you tuned the whole universe, and you watch over every detail of my life. I lay down my own cleverness and trust in your wisdom. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: God set precise laws in the universe, and in the Bible he set the standard of truth for my life.
Humility: I don't have to understand everything before I trust. A wisdom that amazes even physicists is worthy of my confident surrender.
Let Jesus receive the glory: when I see something exquisite, I give the praise to the Designer, not to coincidence.

blocks.h: This week: write down three things you once thought were coincidences but now see as God's arrangement, and share one of them with a friend.
Quiz

quiz.q: What would happen if the cosmological constant were several hundred times larger?
o: The universe would expand too fast for galaxies to form
quiz.e: Weinberg's 1987 estimate showed that the cosmological constant must be very small for galaxies to have a chance to form.

quiz.q: What is the current scientific status of the “multiverse”?
o: Theoretical speculation with no direct observational evidence
quiz.e: The multiverse is theoretical speculation, and we honestly label it as still under study.

quiz.q: Which attribute of God does this unit mainly reveal?
quiz.e: “He has established the world by his wisdom.” (Jeremiah 10:12)

units.title: The Vast Starry Sky
units.sub: From the earth to the edge of the observable universe, step by step we measure the heavens made by God's hand.

share.v: Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these, who brings out their army by number. He calls them all by name.

blocks.h: Light can circle the earth seven and a half times in one second. Yet light from the farthest reaches of the universe has traveled for more than ten billion years to reach our eyes.

Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these, who brings out their army by number. He calls them all by name. By the greatness of his might, and because he is strong in power, not one is lacking.
A patch of sky the size of a grain of sand

In 1995, the Hubble Space Telescope pointed at a tiny, seemingly empty patch of sky near the Big Dipper and photographed it continuously for ten days. That patch was only about one 24-millionth of the whole sky, like a grain of sand held at arm's length. Yet about three thousand galaxies appeared in the picture.
If each galaxy were a city, that sand-grain-sized patch of sky would be packed with three thousand cities, and each city would be home to a hundred billion stars or more.
How many galaxies are there?

Our own Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across and holds 100 to 400 billion stars. The number of galaxies in the observable universe is estimated at somewhere between several hundred billion and more than a trillion.

The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across. That is larger than “the age of the universe × the speed of light,” because space itself has been expanding while the light was on its way.

A 2016 study estimated that there may be as many as two trillion galaxies; in 2021, New Horizons measured the cosmic background light from beyond Pluto and arrived at a much lower estimate, about several hundred billion. This is science's ongoing process of correction at work.
The Hubble Deep Field image captured about three thousand galaxies in a tiny region of sky.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach the earth; the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.24 light-years away; the Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away.
The number of galaxies in the observable universe is roughly several hundred billion to more than a trillion; estimates from different methods still differ widely.

The vastness of the universe does not mean human beings are unimportant; on the contrary, the Bible says the God who made all the host of heaven cares especially for people. This is a declaration of faith, and the heart of this unit.
His eternal power: the God who counts the stars
He counts the number of the stars. He calls them all by their names.
Humanity, with its best telescopes, still cannot count how many galaxies there are; yet God can call every star by name. However big the universe is, his power is bigger still.

Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and marked off the sky with his span, and calculated the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?
What comes next in the same passage

Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel, “My way is hidden from Yahweh, and the justice due me is disregarded by my God”? … He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might.
Right after Isaiah speaks of the vast starry sky, he turns to people who are weary. The God who counts the stars also counts your tears.
Look up at the sky tonight and try counting how many stars you can see. Then remember: he can call every one of them by name, and he can call you by name too.
Reflect: How big are my troubles when set within the universe? And how big are they before God?

Prayer: Lord, you mark off the heavens with the span of your hand, and my burden is not heavy in your hands. Please give strength to me in my weariness, and let me mount up with wings like an eagle. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Focus on Jesus: not on myself, not on others, not on my circumstances. I look to the Lord who is greater than the universe.
From an earthly perspective to a heavenly one: the problem hasn't gotten smaller, but I see that God is bigger.
Humility overcomes pride: under the vast starry sky, no one can go on thinking they are great.

blocks.h: This week: find a friend who is going through a weary season, send them Isaiah 40:26–31, and pray for them.
Quiz

quiz.q: About how many galaxies did the Hubble Deep Field capture in a tiny patch of sky?
quiz.e: About three thousand galaxies, and that patch of sky was like a grain of sand seen at arm's length.

quiz.q: About how long does sunlight take to travel from the sun to the earth?
quiz.e: About 8 minutes 20 seconds; light from Proxima Centauri takes 4.24 years.

quiz.q: After describing the starry sky, whom does Isaiah 40 go on to comfort?
o: People who are weary and weak
quiz.e: “He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might.” (Isaiah 40:29)

units.title: Let There Be Light
units.sub: The first words of creation were “Let there be light.” The mysteries of light still amaze physicists today.

share.v: God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.

blocks.h: Every color you are seeing right now is light. Yet the light the human eye can see is only a very narrow slice of the whole electromagnetic spectrum.

Even more wonderful: the band where the sun gives off the most energy, the band where the atmosphere is most transparent, the band where water is most transparent, and the band our eyes can see almost all overlap in the same narrow window.
God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
The universe's speed limit
The speed of light in a vacuum is 299,792,458 meters per second. This value never changes, and since 1983 it has been used directly to define how long “one meter” is.
Light is like the universe's messenger. Because the messenger takes time to travel, every star we see is showing us “how it used to look”: the farther we look, the older the universe we see.
A just-right window

Visible light has wavelengths of roughly 380 to 750 nanometers. The peak of the sun's radiation falls right here; earth's atmosphere is almost transparent in this band while absorbing much of the harmful ultraviolet and some of the infrared; and water is transparent only in this band, which lets life in the oceans carry out photosynthesis.

The energy range photosynthesis needs, and the energy range needed by the light-sensitive molecules in our eyes, also fall within the same window. Biochemist Michael Denton calls this a chain of astonishing “coincidences.”

Each of these phenomena has a physical explanation; for example, the energies at which molecules absorb light naturally fall in this range. But the question is: why do the laws of nature happen to make so many conditions favorable to life at the same time?
The speed of light in a vacuum is 299,792,458 meters per second, a constant defined by the International System of Units.
The farther we look, the earlier the universe we see: light from the Andromeda Galaxy has been traveling for about 2.5 million years.
Earth's atmosphere and liquid water are both fairly transparent in the visible band and strongly absorbing in many other bands.
That so many favorable conditions fall within the same narrow window points to purposeful design. This is a philosophical inference, and scholars differ on what it means.
God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
His divine nature: goodness and holiness
Light makes all things visible, and it lets life grow. God placed light on the first day of creation, as if to say: I am giving you a world you can see and live in. This is his goodness.
In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it.
I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.
seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
Paul connects the first light of Genesis with the moment a person comes to faith. In the beginning God lit up the universe; today he lights up the human heart.
Tomorrow morning, watch the first sunlight come into your room. That light left the sun a little over eight minutes earlier and traveled all that way for you.
Reflect: Is there a corner of my heart where I still don't want to let the light in?
Prayer: Lord Jesus, you are the light of the world. Please shine into the darkness in my heart, and make me a light for others. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Holy Spirit is my guide: light does not shine on everything to show off, but so people can see the path clearly. I ask the Holy Spirit to light up my next step.
Live out the life of Christ: “You are the light of the world.” Let people see my good works and glorify my Father in heaven (Matthew 5:14–16).
Selflessness: light does not shine for itself; it lights up others.

blocks.h: This week: do one good deed without expecting anything back, and let someone's life be a little brighter because of you.
Quiz

quiz.q: Why do we say “the farther we look, the earlier the universe we see”?
o: Because light takes time to travel
quiz.e: Light from far away takes a long time to arrive, so we see things as they were when the light set out.

quiz.q: Which of the following also falls within the narrow window of visible light?
o: The bands where water and the atmosphere are most transparent
The band used by cell phone signals
quiz.e: The peak of solar radiation and the transparency windows of the atmosphere and water all overlap with visible light.

quiz.q: Which verse says “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all”?
quiz.e: 1 John 1:5.

units.title: The Furnace of the Stars
units.sub: The carbon, oxygen and iron in our bodies were all forged inside stars.

share.v: when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?

blocks.h: The iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones, the carbon in every cell: none of it was made on earth. It was forged in the cores of ancient stars at temperatures of many millions of degrees.
God formed man from “the dust of the ground,” and that dust, it turns out, was fired in the furnaces of the stars.
Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Where do the elements come from?

items: Hydrogen, helium (and a little lithium): formed in the first few minutes after the beginning of the universe.
Carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, up to iron: in the cores of stars, lighter nuclei fuse into heavier ones.
Elements heavier than iron (such as gold and iodine): produced in supernova explosions and neutron star collisions.

blocks.h: In 1957, Margaret and Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle published a classic paper that fully explained how stars make the elements. In 2017, astronomers for the first time observed a collision of two neutron stars with both gravitational waves and light, and watched heavy elements being formed.
The miracle of carbon

To form carbon, three helium nuclei must collide almost at the same moment, which should be extremely difficult. In 1953, Hoyle reasoned that the carbon nucleus must have a state at a specific energy (about 7.65 million electron volts) for carbon to be produced in large amounts. Laboratory experiments soon found exactly that state, now called the “Hoyle state.”

Hoyle himself did not believe in God, yet in 1981 he wrote that a common-sense interpretation of the facts suggests that a superintellect has “monkeyed” with physics, as well as with chemistry and biology.

Later studies have shown that the yields of carbon and oxygen are quite sensitive to the energy of the Hoyle state and the strength of the nuclear force, though precise estimates of that sensitivity are still debated.
Most elements heavier than helium were formed inside stars and in stellar explosions.
Neutron star collisions produce heavy elements such as gold; this was observed directly in 2017.
The carbon nucleus has the excited state Hoyle predicted, which allows stars to produce carbon efficiently.
The yields of carbon and oxygen are sensitive to slight changes in the nuclear force; the degree of sensitivity is still being studied.
His wisdom: a gift long in the making

Before human beings appeared, stars had burned and exploded generation after generation, preparing the materials for life. God is never in a hurry; what he prepares for us is earlier and more thorough than we can imagine.
For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.
There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for one star differs from another star in glory.
Paul uses the differing glory of the stars to explain the glory of the resurrection body. We who came from dust will, through Christ, one day receive glorious, imperishable bodies.
Put your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat. Every atom in this body has gone through God's long and careful preparation.
Reflect: I am dust, yet I carry God's breath; I am small, yet I am treasured by God.
Prayer: Father, thank you that long before I was born, you were already preparing for me. My life is your gift, and I want to offer it back to you for your use. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Humility: I am dust; I have nothing to boast about.
Dignity: I carry God's breath and am made in God's image; I don't need to feel worthless.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry: God spent ages preparing the materials of life; I too will patiently let God shape my life.

blocks.h: This week: say to a friend who often feels inferior, “You are a work God carefully prepared.”
Quiz

quiz.q: Where was most of the carbon in our bodies formed?
o: In the depths of the ocean
quiz.e: Carbon is formed in the cores of stars by the fusion of helium nuclei.

quiz.q: The “Hoyle state” is connected with the formation of which element?
quiz.e: This energy state of the carbon nucleus allows stars to produce carbon in large amounts.

quiz.q: What event did astronomers observe in 2017 that confirmed the formation of heavy elements?
o: A collision of two neutron stars
quiz.e: The neutron star collision was observed with both gravitational waves and light.

units.title: A Place to See the Universe
units.sub: Earth is not only fit to live on; it also happens to be an excellent place to observe the universe.

share.v: that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us.

blocks.h: The sun's diameter is about 400 times the moon's, and the sun is also about 400 times farther from the earth than the moon is. So, seen from earth, the moon can cover the sun exactly, without covering too much.
This means that during a total solar eclipse, scientists can see the corona around the sun, and can even see stars next to the sun in the daytime.
God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years;
A total eclipse confirmed relativity

In 1919, British astronomer Arthur Eddington and his colleagues used a total solar eclipse to photograph stars near the sun, and found that starlight passing the sun was bent by an amount that matched the prediction of Einstein's general relativity. This observation made relativity world-famous.

The moon moves about 3.8 centimeters farther from the earth each year. In the distant past the moon was closer, and in the far future it will be farther away, and then there will be no more perfect total eclipses. Human beings happen to live in the era when perfect total eclipses can be seen.
A good location in the Milky Way

The solar system lies between the Milky Way's spiral arms: not in a crowded, dangerous place like the galactic core, nor at the edge where heavy elements are scarce. Astronomers call such a region the “galactic habitable zone.”

This location also gives us a clear view, less obscured by dust, of distant galaxies and the cosmic background radiation. Astronomer Guillermo Gonzalez and philosopher Jay Richards argue that the places best suited for life also happen to be best suited for observation, and that this does not look like coincidence.

Critics see this as a “selection effect”: observers able to think about these questions could only ever appear in suitable places. Supporters reply that a selection effect can explain habitability but does not necessarily explain why the same place is also suited for observation.
The sun's diameter is about 400 times the moon's, and its distance is also about 400 times greater, so during a total eclipse the two appear nearly the same size.
During the 1919 total eclipse, starlight was observed to be bent by the sun's gravity, supporting general relativity.
The moon moves about 3.8 centimeters farther from the earth each year (by laser ranging).
The Milky Way contains a “galactic habitable zone” better suited to complex life; its extent is still debated.
“Habitability and observability are correlated” is a disputed philosophical argument.

He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us.
His goodness: an open window
God did not only give people a home; he also gave them a window, so they could look out on the universe and understand his works. He wants to be found.
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge.

Paul said this in Athens to philosophers who did not know God. He began with the created world they were familiar with and ended with Jesus rising from the dead (Acts 17:31). That is exactly the path this app follows.
The place where you live and the era you were born into are all part of God's arrangement. He put you here so that you would seek him.
Reflect: What window has God opened in my life to let me see him?
Prayer: Lord, you are not far from me. Thank you for determining my times and my boundaries. Help me seek you and glorify you right where I am. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Build God's kingdom system: God has placed me in my family, my workplace and my city, and those places are territory of his kingdom.
Let Jesus reign: my boundaries are not an accident but his arrangement; within them I obey him.
Relationships matter more than things: God lets people “reach out for him and find him,” and I want to become a window through which others come to know God.

blocks.h: This week: look up the next solar or lunar eclipse visible where you live, and invite a friend to watch it with you.
Quiz

quiz.q: Why can the moon, seen from earth, cover the sun exactly?
o: The sun's diameter and distance are both about 400 times the moon's
The moon is bigger than the sun
quiz.e: The two factors of about 400 cancel out, so the two look the same size.

quiz.q: Which theory did the 1919 total eclipse observations support?
quiz.e: Starlight was bent by the sun's gravity, as Einstein predicted.

quiz.q: According to Acts 17, why does God determine people's times and boundaries?
o: So that people would seek God
So that people would be afraid
So that people would compare themselves with one another
quiz.e: “that they should seek the Lord… though he is not far from each one of us.”

units.title: The Ordinances of Heaven and Earth
units.sub: The same laws govern everything from the earth to the ends of the universe. Science is possible because the universe is orderly.

share.v: It is because of Yahweh's loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn't fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

blocks.h: In 1846, before any astronomer had seen Neptune, they worked out its position with pen and paper. When the telescope was pointed in that direction, there Neptune was.

In 2015, scientists detected gravitational waves given off by the merger of two black holes more than a billion years ago, waves predicted by Einstein's equations back in 1916. The universe keeps its rules, and keeps them astonishingly well.
While the earth remains, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease.
The same laws everywhere

Analyzing the spectra of distant galaxies, astronomers find that atoms there absorb and emit light exactly as they do in laboratories on earth. The laws of physics billions of light-years away are the same as the laws here.
It is like a dictionary: whether you open it in Taipei or in London, every word means the same thing. Every corner of the universe uses the same “dictionary of laws.”
Why does mathematics work?

In 1960, Nobel laureate in physics Eugene Wigner wrote a famous essay describing the effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences as “unreasonable”: mathematics worked out by people on paper somehow describes the motions of distant heavenly bodies with precision.

The pioneers of modern science, such as Kepler and Newton, believed the universe was made by a rational God, and was therefore worth studying and able to be understood. To them, studying nature meant thinking the Creator's thoughts after him.

Whether the physical constants have changed very slightly over the history of the universe is still a research question. Current observations restrict any possible change in the fine-structure constant to a very small range, and there is as yet no accepted evidence of change.
Neptune was discovered in 1846 at the position predicted by mathematics.
Gravitational waves were first detected directly in 2015, in agreement with the predictions of general relativity.
The spectra of distant objects show that the physical constants are extremely uniform across the universe; whether there are extremely small changes is still being studied.
The best explanation for the order and intelligibility of the universe is a rational and faithful Creator. This is a philosophical inference.
His divine nature: faithfulness

Yahweh, who gives the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, who stirs up the sea, so that its waves roar; Yahweh of Armies is his name, says: “If these ordinances depart from before me,” says Yahweh, “then the offspring of Israel also will cease from being a nation before me forever.”

God uses the laws of the universe as a guarantee of his promises: as long as the sun and moon keep to their ordinances, his covenant with his people will not fail. Every sunrise speaks of God's faithfulness.
His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power.
What scientists call the “laws of nature,” the Bible calls Jesus' “word of his power.” The universe is not a machine that runs by itself; it is upheld by Christ at every moment.
Tomorrow morning when you see the sunrise, say to God, “Great is your faithfulness!”
Reflect: God never breaks faith in the universe; how could his promises to me fail?
Prayer: Faithful Lord, you uphold all things, and you uphold me. Just as the sun and moon keep your ordinances, I want to follow you faithfully every day. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: the universe has its ordinances, and my life also needs God's word as its ordinance.
The eight steps of changing our mindset: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, multiplication. Practice them regularly, and your life will change.
Faithfulness: keep your word as God does, do what you say, and become someone others can rely on.

blocks.h: This week: set a fixed daily time for devotions, and keep it for seven days in a row.
Quiz

quiz.q: How was Neptune discovered?
o: Its position was calculated mathematically first, then it was observed
A spacecraft photographed it by chance
Ancient people saw it with the naked eye
quiz.e: It was discovered in 1846 at the position predicted by mathematics.

quiz.q: How did Wigner describe the effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences?
quiz.e: It is astonishing that human mathematics can describe the universe so precisely.

quiz.q: According to Hebrews 1:3, what upholds all things?
quiz.e: “upholding all things by the word of his power.”

units.title: New Heavens and a New Earth
units.sub: The universe had a beginning and is heading toward an end. But the Bible's story does not stop at heat death; it ends in renewal.

share.v: But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.

blocks.h: In 1998, two teams of astronomers observing distant supernovae found that the universe's expansion is not slowing down but actually speeding up. Three scientists received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for this.
According to our current understanding, the universe will grow ever colder and darker. The stars will go out one by one, until only cold and silence remain. This is called “heat death.”
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
Everything is “wearing out”

The second law of thermodynamics says that the usable energy in a closed system keeps decreasing, and disorder (entropy) only ever increases. Hot water cools, a room left alone gets messy, and stars eventually use up their fuel.
In about 5 billion years, our sun will swell into a red giant. In the far more distant future, stars in the universe will gradually stop forming and finally go dark.
The universe is like a wound-up clock that has been ticking since the beginning, its spring slowly unwinding. That tells us two things: it was once wound up, and it will not keep running forever.

The ultimate fate of the universe depends on the nature of dark energy. Most models predict endless expansion and gradual cooling; some models discuss other possibilities. All of these are projections based on the laws we know, and they are still being studied.
The universe's expansion is accelerating (1998 supernova observations; 2011 Nobel Prize).
In about 5 billion years the sun will leave the main sequence and swell into a red giant.
The long-term fate of the universe is most likely continued expansion and gradual cooling, a “heat death,” but this depends on the nature of dark energy.
The universe itself cannot offer eternal hope; hope must come from outside the universe. This is a declaration of faith.
They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same. Your years will have no end.
The groaning of creation

that the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now.
His eternity and righteousness: making all things new
But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.

He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away. He who sits on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.”
The Lord who gave the universe its beginning will also give it a new beginning. The resurrection of Jesus is the first light of dawn of the new creation.
What in your life is “wearing out”? Your health, your relationships, your dreams? Bring them before the Lord who is “making all things new.”
Reflect: Am I living for a heaven and earth that will pass away, or for a kingdom that will last forever?
Prayer: Eternal Lord, your years have no end. Turn my eyes from the temporary to the eternal. May your kingdom come, and your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: From a temporary perspective to an eternal one: measure today's gains and losses with the ruler of eternity.
Become an overcomer: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne.” (Revelation 3:21)
Welcome the Lord's return: build God's kingdom system, prepare for the new heavens and new earth, and let God's kingdom come in my family and my workplace.

blocks.h: This week: write down one thing you will do “for eternity,” and start on it this week.

Congratulations on completing the Cosmos Hall! From “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” to “I am making all things new,” you have seen the story of the whole universe, and you have seen the hero of the story: Jesus Christ.
Quiz

quiz.q: In 1998, astronomers discovered that the universe's expansion is…?
quiz.e: Observations of distant supernovae showed that the expansion is speeding up.

quiz.q: What does the second law of thermodynamics tell us?
quiz.e: Disorder only increases; the universe is wearing out like a garment.

quiz.q: What ending does the Bible give to the story of the universe?
o: New heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells
quiz.e: “Behold, I am making all things new.” (Revelation 21:5)

questions.q: Where did the universe come from?
Why is the universe just right for life?
The universe is so vast: do I still matter?
Must science and faith be in conflict?
How will the universe end? Is there any hope?
